pages.text:
*Sky Report: falling glass, swirling gusts, sky the color of an old bruise.*

Marra called the Elders together. They huddled in a low, murmuring knot, wings twitching. The air smelled of salt and ozone. When Marra spoke, her voice cut through the growing wind. "The season is short. The Trial goes on."

A ripple of excitement spread through the crowd. Then she paused, her grey head tilting toward the small brown sparrow on the branch. "Pip may enter. On the strength of what we have just seen."

A few fledglings cheered, sharp and quick. Others grumbled, shifting their weight. Cinder looked away, preening a chestnut feather with exaggerated care. Uncle Dorn said nothing. He did not grumble or cheer. He simply moved one step closer to Pip, his plump body blocking a gust that tried to lift her off the branch. He stayed there, solid and warm, like a stone anchor in a rushing stream. Pip leaned into him, just for a second, before straightening her wings.
pages.image: A tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail stands on a branch, leaning slightly toward a plump grey sparrow who is blocking the wind; in the background, a crowd of sparrows watches a large elder sparrow.

pages.text:
Cinder flew first. He was magnificent. He hit the Windmill spiral with a grace that made the air seem to part for him. The Marsh Wind, usually a tricky, twisting lane, was sliced clean and straight by his powerful wings. When he reached the Cliffs, he did not ride the updraft. He fought it. He roared into the rising air, muscles bulging, forcing his way up until he landed exactly on the marker twig, not a feather's width off.

The hedge erupted. Two hundred sparrows shrieked and cheered, a sound like wind through dry reeds. Cinder preened, his chestnut feathers glossy in the dying light. He glanced down at Pip. There was no mockery in his eyes this time. It was something colder, or perhaps just tired. He looked at her, then at the darkening sky, and turned his back. The respect was there, but it was distant, like a star that had burned out.
pages.image: A large glossy chestnut sparrow lands perfectly on a high twig on a cliff edge, wings spread; below, a crowd of sparrows cheers; a tiny brown sparrow watches from a lower branch.

pages.text:
Pip flew last, when the wind had stopped being a friend and started acting like a grumpy uncle. It twisted and turned, refusing to be read, and spun her in the Windmill lanes until she was dizzy. She had to fight every inch of the line. The Marsh Wind was a maze of gusts, so she trusted Nettle, who stood on the reeds pointing with one wing. Left. Right. Hold. Pip followed the instructions, beating her wings hard against the push.

Then came the Cliffs. Pip went up, higher and higher, much higher than Cinder had managed. The air turned cold and sharp, tasting like winter. For one bright moment, she saw the whole hedge from above, just a tiny patch of green in a vast white sea. Then a gust ripped her sideways. She tumbled, wings beating against the empty sky, unable to hold her shape. She landed far from the marker, on a jagged rock. She was not clean. She was not first. She was last.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow tumbles through swirling white wind against a grey sky, wings flapping wildly; far below, a cliff edge and a small green hedge are visible; a skinny sparrow watches from the cliffs.

pages.text:
The silence after Pip landed was heavy. It was not the silence of awe, but of exhaustion. Pip’s legs trembled. Her chest heaved, each breath a small, painful effort. She did not look at the scores. She did not look at the Elders. She had done it. She had flown the course, on the day, in front of everyone. That was enough. That had to be enough.

Uncle Dorn landed beside her. He did not say "small birds stay low." He did not say "I told you so." He simply pressed his feathers against hers. It was a small, warm, solid touch. It was the first time he had touched her without a warning attached. Pip closed her eyes and leaned into the warmth, the wind still howling around them, but the small space between them was quiet.
pages.image: A plump grey sparrow presses its feathers gently against a tiny, exhausted brown sparrow with a crooked tail; they stand close together on a rock while wind blows around them.

pages.text:
Marra’s voice boomed, but it sounded thin in the rising wind. "The new Storm-Sparrows are Cinder, and two others." The names were called. Not Pip. The words hit her like a stone, cold and hard. Marra added, "Pip has shown remarkable skill. The Elders will consider her again in a season or two."

Pip felt the sting of it, but it was distant. She was too tired to be angry. Too tired to be sad. From a rooftop far above, Old Tuck’s dry, raspy voice drifted down. "Ah, well. They will be needing you sooner than they think."

Pip looked up. Behind Tuck, the western sky had turned the color of iron. The bruise was spreading, dark and deep, swallowing the last of the light. The air smelled of rain that had not yet fallen.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow looks up at a one-eyed, ragged sparrow perched on a high rocky ledge of the split oak tree; behind them, the sky is dark and purple, swirling with storm clouds.
